title: Tamsin and the Winter
premise: Coral Blackwood, a property surveyor sent to appraise the derelict Tamsin House before auction, discovers the building answers his measurements with corrections of its own. His sleep recordings capture a second voice—Tamsin, a girl drowned in the well by the town's founding families in 1911, still waiting for someone to sing her harvest song to its final verse so she can name her killers and rest. But the verse demands a singer's own memory as payment: whoever completes it relives their worst act of complicity in full. Coral, who once falsified a survey that condemned a family's home, must decide whether truth or self-preservation wins—and on the harvest moon he sings the last verse, surrenders his secret, and frees Tamsin, though the house keeps one recording of his confession as its new tenant.
about_author: Casper Sandoval is the pen name of a former rural assessor who spent a decade appraising abandoned properties across the northern counties and never slept well in any of them. They write horror about buildings that remember what people prefer to forget.

chapters.title: The Square Footage of Silence
chapters.summary: POV Coral. Coral arrives at Tamsin House for a routine pre-auction appraisal; every room measures slightly larger than it should, and the front door count changes between visits. He rationalizes it as settling foundations. Emotional beat: professional detachment beginning to crack as the house demonstrates it notices him back.

chapters.title: Doors Counted at Midnight
chapters.summary: POV Coral. Following his own protocol, Coral counts doors each night and leaves a recorder running while he sleeps. The playback catches a child's voice answering questions he never asked aloud, correcting his measurements by name. Emotional beat: dread curdling into obsessive curiosity—he stops wanting to leave.

chapters.title: What the Well Kept
chapters.summary: POV Coral, with archival interludes. Researching the estate, Coral finds the 1911 drowning of Tamsin Vale, blamed on an accident, and learns the town's founding families sealed the well rather than fill it. The recorder now plays fragments of a harvest song, always stopping before the last verse. Emotional beat: the pull of justice for the dead versus the safety of walking away.

chapters.title: The Second Voice
chapters.summary: POV Coral. The voice begins addressing Coral directly through the recordings, asking whether he has ever lied on paper. He denies it; the house responds by replaying sounds of his own past—his falsified survey that displaced the Okafor family. Emotional beat: guilt surfacing, loyalty to his own reputation warring with the truth.

chapters.title: Neighbors Who Look Away
chapters.summary: POV Coral. Coral interviews elderly locals; they know exactly what happened in 1911 and have collectively agreed to forget, warning him that singing the song's end 'brings everyone's harvest due.' One woman slips him a handwritten first three verses. Emotional beat: horror at communal complicity—the whole town is the house's accomplice.

chapters.title: Verse by Verse
chapters.summary: POV Coral. Testing the song, Coral sings the first verse alone; the temperature drops and Tamsin shows him a memory not his own—the night she was held under. Each verse costs the singer a memory of their own choosing. Emotional beat: mounting cost made explicit; Coral realizes the final verse will take his worst one.

chapters.title: The Auction Notice
chapters.summary: POV Coral. His firm, pressured by the founding families' descendants, orders Coral to certify the house structurally sound and free of encumbrance—effectively erasing Tamsin again. His loyalty to his career demands compliance. Emotional beat: the trap closes; justice outside the law means risking everything legal protection would grant him.

chapters.title: Harvest Moon Rising
chapters.summary: POV Coral. On the eve of the full moon, the descendants arrive to celebrate the sale, and the house begins sealing doors, counting them down like a verdict. Tamsin's voice asks Coral one last time if he'll sing. Emotional beat: terror and resolve fused; Coral chooses the truth over invisibility.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: POV Coral. Before the assembled descendants, Coral sings the final verse, surrendering his memory of the Okafors' eviction—living it fully, weeping, naming his lie aloud. The house turns its attention to the descendants, whose own inherited secrets surface as the walls recite them. Emotional beat: cathartic reckoning; the song completes and the well opens.

chapters.title: Appraised at Last
chapters.summary: POV Coral, weeks later. Tamsin is gone; the house stands empty and finally measures true. Coral files a corrected report, loses his license, and finds he sleeps soundly for the first time—except the house mailed him one cassette: his confession, kept as its permanent record. Emotional beat: bittersweet peace; some truths are preserved even after they're freed.
